name: Nose shaper clip (Trados Model 25)

card.summary: An early-1900s mechanical nose-shaping clip worn on the nose to press it toward a straighter or slimmer shape, the ancestor of the nose clips sold online today.
card.note: Users report any change in shape lasts a short time and can leave redness; historic devices could cause sleep disturbance and skin injury.

quick.overview:
The Trados Model 25 was one of a family of mechanical nose shapers sold in the early twentieth century. A metal and padded clip was worn on the nose, often at night, and tightened to press the nose toward a straighter, slimmer or less crooked shape without surgery.
Similar devices were sold in Europe from the 1890s, such as the Zello-Punkt Model 21, and clips on retail sites are marketed in the same way today. Reports from a historian who tried an older device and from forum users describe only short-lived changes in shape, and no clinical trials exist.
quick.how: The historical devices were fitted over the nose with adjusting screws and held with a head band or similar, and makers advised long regular wear over months. Modern clips are worn for set periods and are mostly discussed as a non-surgical alternative to rhinoplasty.
quick.risks: The Zello-Punkt tester reported sleep disturbance and facial injuries from sharp metal edges. Forum users of modern clips report temporary shape change and redness. Anyone with breathing problems or a nasal injury would consult a clinician.

lead: Nose shapers were mechanical devices sold in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries to reshape the nose without surgery. The Trados Model 25 is one such device, catalogued as a steel-and-cotton clip; a medical-history library record attributes it to a Binghamton, New York seller who billed himself a nose-shaping specialist. Little else about it is documented.

A better documented relative is the Zello-Punkt Model 21, introduced in 1894 and patented by Professor G. von Eck: a moulded brass shell shaped like a nose pyramid with adjusting screws, a front plate and a thin leather cushion, held on with a rubber band around the head [1]. It was marketed for straightening crooked, humped, potato or saddle noses, and sold through hairdressers and pharmacies [1].

The idea persists in modern clips sold online. On looksmax.org a poster asked whether consistent use of nose shaping clips would give a smaller nose, and replies said any change in shape lasts a short time and leaves the nose red [2].

chain: Clip presses the nose from the sides or bridge
Tissue is held in a straighter or narrower position while worn
Nose looks slimmer or straighter (temporary, per users)
angle.text: The clip is worn in the hope of narrowing or straightening the nose without surgery. People who use modern versions describe it as a non-surgical alternative to rhinoplasty.

infobox: Late 1800s to early 1900s; modern versions sold online
Steel and cotton (Trados 25); brass and leather (Zello-Punkt) [1]

paras: The Zello-Punkt had a brass outer shell with adjusting screws, an adjustable front plate and leather-cushioned inner plates, secured with a rubber band [1]. Its manual advised rubbing the nasal skin with a special wax to soften the cartilage and wearing the device as often as possible for several months [1]. It was sold alongside other grooming aids, and wearers were nicknamed people with golden noses [1].

A modern ENT writer who tried a Zello-Punkt doubted it could produce a lasting result, because the pressure seemed to depend on the head band and the tissue could be compressed only for a few minutes; he reported sleep disturbance and facial injuries from sharp metal edges [1]. Forum users of current clips report that the nose changes shape for a short period and goes red afterward [2].

timeline.event: Zello-Punkt Model 21 nose shaper introduced and patented by G. von Eck [1]
